A wise or learned person seeking human wisdom, in contrast to divine miracles
G1672.detail: 1. A Greek is primarily a person from Greece or who speaks Greek, in contrast to a barbarian (one who does not speak Greek) and a Jew (John 7:35 speaks of the Greeks dispersed among whom the Jews expected Jesus to teach). 2. In the New Testament, the term often refers to a non-Jewish Gentile, particularly those who frequented synagogues or were associated with the Jewish faith — the "God-fearing Greeks" mentioned in Acts 17:4 are an example. 3. Sometimes the term takes on a more figurative meaning: a Greek represents one who seeks human wisdom and reason, while a Jew seeks miracles (1 Corinthians 1:22) — this is why Paul contrasts Greeks with Barbarians in Romans 1:14, marking a cultural and moral distinction.
G1672.origine: The Greek word Hellēn comes from Hellas, the name of ancient Greece. It designates the quintessential Greek people, cultured, speaking Greek, and representing classical Mediterranean civilization. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the term Iavan (Joel 3:6, Zechariah 9:13) is often used to refer to Greece and the Greeks — this people symbolizes for the Jews wisdom, culture, and the strangeness of the Gentile world.
G1672.emploi: The word appears about 25 times in the New Testament, particularly in the Gospel of John, the Acts of the Apostles, and the epistles of Paul. It designates non-Jews of Greek or Hellenized culture, numerous in the cities of the Roman Empire. Paul uses the phrase "Jews and Greeks" to express the universality of salvation (Romans 1:16, 1 Corinthians 12:13, Galatians 3:28), showing that the Gospel is addressed to all nations without distinction. Sometimes the term extends to Gentiles in general (Acts 19:17 speaks of Greeks in Ephesus), and sometimes it designates pagans who worship human wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:22).
G1672.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the Gospel is not reserved for Jews but is addressed to all nations and peoples. It invites recognition that God welcomes both the Greek and the Jew, the learned and the ignorant (Romans 1:14), provided they turn to Christ. It is a call to the universality of salvation and the unity of the Church beyond cultural and religious boundaries.

sens: Belonging to Greece or Greek culture
Written or spoken in the Greek language
G1673.detail:
1. An adjective that qualifies what comes from Greece or pertains to Greek civilization. Luke 23:38 shows the inscription on the cross written in three languages, including Greek, which testifies to the presence and influence of Greek culture in the Mediterranean world of the 1st century.

2. Expressed or written in the Greek language. In Revelation 9:11, the angel of the abyss has a name "in the Greek language": Apollyon, which means destroyer — it is the Greek that conveys the meaning of the name for the Greek-speaking readers of Revelation.
G1673.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek *Hellēnès* (the Greeks), the people who inhabited Greece. The adjective *Hellēnikos* (Greek) is regularly formed by adding the suffix *-ikos*, which creates adjectives of relation or belonging. All adjectives in this family refer to Greece and its culture: this is the word the New Testament uses to designate everything Greek, in contrast to Hebrew, Aramaic, or Latin.
G1673.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In Luke 23:38, it qualifies the language in which the inscription above Jesus on the cross is written: it is in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek. In Revelation 9:11, it designates the language in which the name of the angel of the abyss, Apollyon, sounds — the text specifies that this name has a Greek meaning. These two usages show that the term applies mainly to the language rather than to a people or an abstract nationality: it is a concrete way of saying "in Greek."
G1673.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospel was written in Greek and addresses a world where Greek was the common language. The presence of Greek on the cross of Jesus and in the book of Revelation shows that the Good News was not reserved for Jews but intended for all peoples of the Roman Empire, particularly the Greeks. This underscores the universality of salvation in Christ.

sens: A woman of Greek culture and language
A non-Jewish woman, of pagan religion
G1674.detail: This refers to a woman who belongs to the Greek world, through her culture, language, and often her origin. In Mark 7:26, the Gospel specifies that the woman who came to ask for healing for her daughter is "Greek by nation" (Syrophoenician by race): she speaks Greek, lives according to Greek customs, and does not practice the Jewish religion. In Acts 17:12, the "distinguished Greek women" are influential women of Greek society who adhere to the Gospel: they also belong to the Greek world but have believed in Jesus. For the Jews of the time, being Greek meant not being Jewish — living outside the law of Moses, in the world of pagan nations.
G1674.origine: The word comes from the Greek root that designates Greece and the Greek people. It is the feminine form of the word that qualifies Greeks in general. In Hebrew, the Jews simply referred to these foreign peoples as "nations" or "Gentiles"; the Greek word here takes its identity from the culture and language that dominated the Mediterranean at the time of the New Testament.
G1674.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Mark 7:26, it describes the Syrophoenician woman who comes to implore Jesus for her daughter possessed by a demon — her condition as a Greek woman, that is, a non-Jew, emphasizes the challenge that Jesus meets in helping her. In Acts 17:12, it designates Athenian women of high social rank who have believed in Paul's message: here too, their identity as Greek women highlights that the Gospel crosses the boundaries of the Jewish people and reaches the cultured pagans of the Hellenistic world.
G1674.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus never limited his love and power to Jews alone. The Greek woman in Mark 7:26 receives healing despite her status as a foreigner; the Greek women in Acts 17:12 embrace the Gospel: this shows that the Gospel is intended for all peoples, without distinction. It is an encouragement for every believer, regardless of their cultural or religious heritage, to come to Jesus and receive his promises.

sens: Jew who speaks Greek and adopts Greek customs
Member of the Jewish community of Greek language and culture
G1675.detail:
1. An Hellenist is a Jew who has adopted the language, manners, and customs of the Greeks. This is often a Jew from the diaspora, meaning living outside the land of Israel, in regions where Greek was the common language. In Acts 6:1, the Hellenists form a distinct group from the Hebrews (the Aramaic-speaking Jews who remained faithful to Palestinian traditions), which shows that Hellenism was perceived as an adaptation to the culture of the surrounding world.

2. In the early Church, the Hellenists represent the Jews converted to Christ who maintain their Greek and cosmopolitan identity. In Antioch (Acts 11:20), it is the Hellenists who boldly proclaim the Gospel to the Greeks themselves — a daring step that the more conservative Hebrews might not have taken. Among them are great pioneers like Stephen and Philip.
G1675.origine: The word comes from the Greek Hellenizo, which means "to Hellenize" or "to adopt Greek customs." Its root is Hellas (Greece) and Hellenes (the Greeks). The suffix -ist denotes those who practice or adopt something. The term does not exist in the Hebrew of the Old Testament, as it is a reality born after the conquests of Alexander: the Jews dispersed in the Greek empire who gradually absorbed the Greek language and culture.
G1675.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Acts, where it specifically refers to Christian Jews or Jews of Greek language. In Acts 6:1, the "Hellenists" complain because their widows are neglected in the daily assistance provided by the Church — revealing a community tension between two cultural groups within the Jewish people. In Acts 9:29, Paul argues with them (a moment of his early preaching in Jerusalem), showing that they formed a dialoguing group, open to debate. In Acts 11:20, some Hellenists break the cultural barrier by proclaiming the Gospel not only to Hellenized Jews but also to non-Jewish Greeks — a major missionary turning point.
G1675.portee: This word reminds the believer that there are legitimate forms of cultural diversity within the people of God. The Hellenists show that following Jesus does not require abandoning one's language or adopted culture. Their story also encourages Christians to cross boundaries with the Gospel: they were the first to boldly proclaim Christ to the Gentiles, beyond the walls of traditional Judaism. It is a lesson on Christian freedom and the universal mission.

sens: The Greek language
To express oneself in Greek
G1676.detail:
1. The word refers to the Greek language itself, spoken and written in the Mediterranean world. At the cross, the inscription "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" was displayed in three languages — in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (John 19:20) — so that everyone could read it in their own language.
2. By extension, it is used to indicate the act of speaking Greek, of expressing oneself in this language. When the Roman tribune asks Paul, "Do you know Greek?" (Acts 21:37), he is asking if he can communicate in this common language of the entire empire.
G1676.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "Hellèn" which designates a Greek, a man of Greek culture and language, in contrast to the barbarians — all those who spoke other languages. The adverb "Hellénisti" literally means "in the Greek manner" or "in Greek." Greek itself, originating from Athens and the Greek cities, spread everywhere after the conquests of Alexander, becoming the lingua franca of the East. The Greek word often translates the Hebrew "Yavani" in the Greek Old Testament (notably Daniel 8:21, which speaks of the "king of Yavan," Greece).
G1676.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In John 19:20, it qualifies one of the three languages of the inscription on the cross, testifying to the historical reality: Jerusalem was a cosmopolitan city where Greek was common alongside Aramaic and Latin. In Acts 21:37, the Roman tribune addresses Paul, assuming he might speak Greek — a surprise, as the Romans did not expect a captive Jew to master this language. These two passages show that Greek was the language of international communication at the time.
G1676.portee: For the reader, these two verses remind us that Jesus was crucified in a multicultural context where the message had to be proclaimed beyond a single nation. The fact that the New Testament itself is written in Greek underscores the importance of this language for the expansion of the Gospel: God used the lingua franca of the known world so that the Gospel could reach the greatest number.

sens: To attribute to a person, to assign something (an action, a debt, a guilt)
To record on an account, especially a debt account
To assign someone a responsibility, a consequence
G1677.detail:
1. To impute is to put something to someone's account, as one would record an amount in a ledger. It is to attribute to a person an action, a debt, or a fault that becomes theirs in the eyes of the law or morality. In Philemon 1:18, Paul says: "If he owes you anything, put it on my account" — he asks Philemon to record the debt of the young slave Onesimus on his own account, as if he were the one who owed.
2. The word is also used for spiritual realities: to attribute to someone a guilt or a responsibility. In Romans 5:13, Paul explains that "sin is not imputed when there is no law" — without the law to judge it, sin cannot be counted as a transgression against someone. It is a matter of divine recording: does God count sin against man?
3. More broadly, to impute means to assign someone a consequence or a responsibility — to hold someone accountable for an action or a debt.
G1677.origine: The verb comes from the Greek root meaning "to place in accounts" or "to put on account." It is a term from commercial and administrative language: it was used in Egyptian papyri for accounting. In Hebrew, the verb that this word often translates is "chashav" (חשב), which means "to calculate," "to count," "to think" — the image is that of the accountant who records in his books. The Bible primarily uses it to describe how God "counts" or "imputes" actions, faith, or guilt to each person.
G1677.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 5:13, Paul uses it in his theological argument about the relationship between sin and the law: sin exists in the world before the law, but it is not "imputed" — that is, recorded as formal transgression — until the law exists to condemn it. In Philemon 1:18, Paul uses it in a practical and personal context: he asks Philemon to put the debt of Onesimus, the runaway slave, on his own account. These are two uses of the same word: one theological (guilt and law), the other concrete (commercial debt), but both rely on the image of recording or accounting.
G1677.portee: This word shows how God records and counts — it invites the reader to understand that no action remains invisible, that everyone is accountable before a God who "keeps the accounts." In Romans, Paul uses it to explain that grace consists of not imputing sin to the one who believes; in Philemon, he illustrates practical charity: Paul volunteers to bear the debt of another. It is a key word for grasping the justice of God and Christian mercy.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
G1678.detail: Elmadam is a name that appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Luke. He is presented as the father of Er and the son of Kosam, thus occupying his place in the chain of generations that traces back from Jesus to Adam. This name appearing in an official genealogy underscores that Jesus, although the Son of God, is part of a concrete and historical human lineage.
G1678.origine: The name Elmadam is of Hebrew or Aramaic origin. Its exact etymology is uncertain, but it belongs to the type of patronymic names borne by the Hebrews of antiquity. This name appears only once in the biblical texts that have come down to us, making it a rare name in biblical genealogy.
G1678.emploi: Elmadam is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Luke 3:28. Luke inserts this name into his genealogy of Jesus, which traces back from Jesus to Adam. This genealogy differs from the one proposed by Matthew in other details and regularly in several segments. Elmadam represents one of the generations among the ancestors of Jesus on his mother Mary's side, according to the tradition that Luke reports.

sens: To wait for the realization of something in the future, with confidence
To rely on someone or something for it to happen
To wish for something to come to pass or to obtain something
To have hope, to stake one's life or trust on
To anticipate a future event
To nurture a confident expectation, often rooted in faith
G1679.detail:
1. To wait for the realization of something: this is looking towards the future while waiting for what one desires to come to pass. Romans 15:24 gives the image: Paul "hopes" to see the Romans on his way, he truly counts on it happening. It is an expectation directed towards tomorrow, not a mere daydream.

2. To rely on someone or something: this is to place one's trust in a person or reality. In Acts 24:26, the governor "hoped" that Paul would give him money — he relied on it so much that he had him come regularly. It is to put one's support somewhere.

3. To wish to obtain something: to hope is also to desire that a good thing happens for us. In Luke 6:34, lending while hoping to receive in return means giving with the expectation of recovering one's own. The heart looks towards what one would like to have.

4. To place one's faith and trust in: especially in Paul's texts, to hope means to base one's existence, or at least one's deep expectations, on God or Christ. In 1 Timothy 4:10, hoping in God means building one's life on His promise. It is the living hope of the believer.

5. To anticipate an event: this is to expect that something will happen, even without certainty. In Luke 23:8, Herod hoped to see Jesus perform a sign — he expected this, although uncertain.

6. To nurture a faith-based expectation: especially in the deep biblical sense, to hope is to firmly believe in God's promise despite appearances. Hebrews 11:1 states that hope is the substance of things hoped for, the solid assurance of a future that God has promised.
G1679.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "turning one's gaze towards," "stretching towards" something. In ancient Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates terms like "to trust" (בָּטַח) or "to wait patiently" (יָחַל) with this word. Elpizô is not a passive dream: it is an active expectation, a trust that projects towards the future. The Greeks use it for all kinds of waiting; the Bible often makes it the central act of the believer who entrusts himself to God.
G1679.emploi: The verb hope appears 31 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and in the epistles. It is found in three main contexts: first, the expectation of ordinary situations (Paul hopes to come see someone, Acts 26:7; a rich man hopes to do something, 1 Timothy 3:14), then the expectation of material things (Acts 24:26), and finally — this is the most serious and Christian usage — hope in God or in Christ for salvation and resurrection (Romans 15:12; 1 Peter 1:13; 1 Timothy 5:5 which speaks of the widow hoping in God through her prayers). The Letter to the Hebrews offers the synthesis: biblical hope is not a vague wish, it is the substance, the solid assurance of God's promises (Hebrews 11:1). Paul also emphasizes this: Christian hope is patient, it bears all things (1 Corinthians 13:7), and it characterizes the living believer (Romans 8:24-25).
G1679.portee: To hope, for the Christian, is not to close one's eyes or dream of the impossible: it is to firmly turn one's gaze towards God and His promises, accepting not to see the end. This hope gives direction to all of life and changes the heart. It requires an active expectation, a patience that perseveres, and a trust that God will do what He has said. In this, Christian hope is not illusory: it rests on the faithful character of God revealed in the Gospel.

sens: confident expectation of good
joyful certainty of future benefits
firm trust in God and His promises
the good awaited, the object of hope
foundation or reason for hope
God Himself, source of all hope
G1680.detail:
1. Hope is an expectation turned towards the future, filled with trust and desire. It is having a joyful heart because one is waiting for something good: in Acts 2:26, the psalmist rests "with hope," meaning in the confidence that God will act for him.
2. It more broadly designates this joyful certainty of future benefits, particularly the benefits promised by God. In Romans 8:24, "we were saved in hope," which means that our salvation rests on this firm trust in what God will accomplish.
3. For the believers of the New Testament, hope is above all a trust in God and in His Messiah: in 1 Thessalonians 1:3, we speak of "the hope in our Lord Jesus Christ." 
4. Sometimes, the word designates the good itself that one awaits rather than the expectation itself: in Titus 2:13, Jesus Christ is called "the blessed hope," meaning what is hoped for, awaited with joy.
5. Hope can also designate that on which it relies: in 1 Thessalonians 2:19, the converts are the "crown and hope" of the apostle, meaning the reason and foundation of his hope.
6. In Romans 15:13, God is called "the God of hope," showing that hope comes from God and finds its ultimate source in Him.
G1680.origine: The Greek word ἐλπίς comes from a root that evokes waiting and desire. In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew תִּקְוָה (tiqvah, "waiting," "cord"), which refers to the idea of holding on to something. In Hebrew as well, hope is a trust that stands firm. The verb ἐλπίζειν (to hope) derives from it, as does the noun ἐλπιστής (one who hopes). Among the Greeks, the word can designate the expectation of good or bad things, but in the New Testament, it is always positive and turns towards God's promises.
G1680.emploi: Hope appears 47 times in the New Testament, particularly in the Pauline epistles. It first designates the general hope of a future good (Acts 27:20, where one "loses hope" of being saved), then, very quickly, it takes on a religious coloring. In Paul and in the other epistles, it becomes a characteristic virtue of the Christian, based on the resurrection of Christ. The hope of resurrection (Acts 23:6, Romans 4:18) and of eternal life (Titus 1:2) is the highest form of this expectation. It is often associated with faith and charity (1 Corinthians 13:13), forming the three pillars of Christian life. The letter to the Hebrews presents it as an "anchor of the soul" (6:19), an unshakeable certainty. Sometimes, hope is the very object of expectation (what one hopes for), and sometimes it is the attitude of hoping itself.
G1680.portee: Christian hope is not a vague optimism or a mere wish, but a joyful certainty anchored in God and in His promises. It transforms the heart of the believer: in Romans 5:2-5, Paul shows that hope produces perseverance and love. It is a virtue that strengthens in the face of difficulties and sufferings of the present, placing them in the light of what is to come (Romans 15:4). To live this hope, one must base it not on our feelings or circumstances, but on the word of God and on the work accomplished by Christ.

sens: Magician who opposed the apostle Paul in Cyprus
G1681.detail: Elymas is the name of a magician who lived in Cyprus during the time of the apostle Paul. His name means "magician" in Aramaic or Arabic. During Paul and Barnabas's missionary journey on the island, Elymas sought to prevent the proconsul (the Roman governor) from believing in the Gospel (Acts 13:8). Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, denounced him as a fraud and struck him with temporary blindness, which led the proconsul to believe in Jesus.
G1681.origine: The name Elymas comes from Aramaic or Arabic and literally means "magician." It is not the man's real name, but rather a nickname that reveals his activity: he practiced magic and exerted a bad spiritual influence. The Bible itself explains this meaning by saying, "for that is what his name means."
G1681.emploi: Elymas appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:8. He was a false prophet and a Jewish magician who attempted to exert political influence by being near the proconsul Sergius Paulus. His opposition to Paul's preaching illustrates the conflict between the spiritual power of the Gospel and opposing spiritual forces. His judgment by temporary blindness shows God's victory over sorcery and unbelief.
G1681.portee: The story of Elymas teaches that those who actively oppose the Gospel encounter the power of God. It also shows that God can strike those who seek to lead others away from faith, not out of vengeance but to lead to repentance. It is a reminder that God's power surpasses all human or occult powers.

sens: Aramaic exclamation meaning "My God"
G1682.detail: 1. It is an Aramaic exclamation that literally means "My God." Jesus uttered it on the cross at the moment he committed his spirit to God (Mark 15:34). It is an authentically Aramaic word, the language Jesus spoke daily in Galilee, which shows the intensity and authenticity of the moment.
G1682.origine: The word comes from Aramaic אֱלָהּ (elah), which means "God." It is a word from the spoken language in Palestine in the 1st century, closely related to the Hebrew אֱלֹהִים (Elohim). The possessive prefix in Aramaic adds the meaning "my," hence "my God." This very ancient Aramaic word is also the origin of the Arabic word "Allah."
G1682.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in the account of the crucifixion according to Mark (and parallel in Matthew). Jesus cries it out on the cross while quoting Psalm 22 verse 1. The fact that the evangelists preserved this word in Aramaic, instead of translating it, emphasizes its memorable character and the emotional weight of the moment. It is a word that the disciples would never have forgotten hearing.
G1682.portee: This word reveals Jesus' humanity in his moment of extreme distress. By crying out "My God," he expresses not the abandonment of his faith, but the overwhelming weight of separation — perhaps the greatest suffering of the cross. It invites the reader to contemplate the mystery of the passion and to meditate on what Jesus endured for our salvation.

sens: to board a boat by climbing in
to embark on a ship
to begin a journey by water
G1684.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of boarding a vessel, crossing the edge of the boat to settle in. It is a concrete gesture: one lifts a leg, steps over, and hoists oneself aboard. Jesus "went into the boat" (Matthew 8:23), and his disciples followed him.
2. More broadly, the word means "to embark" — that is, to take to the sea, to leave the shore to sail to the other side. When Jesus instructed his disciples to "go into the boat" and to go ahead of him to the other side (Matthew 14:22), he was commanding them to begin the crossing.
3. The verb can also evoke the moment of departure itself, the launch of the journey: after casting out the demons of Gerasa, Jesus "went into the boat" to return (Luke 8:37), thus marking the end of one stage and the beginning of the return.
G1684.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: the prefix "en-" (in) and "baïnô" (to walk, to go). Literally, it means "to go in." The Hebrew word it generally translates is עָלָה (to go up, to ascend), which emphasizes the movement upwards — a natural image for boarding a boat, where one often has to lift their legs to cross the edge.
G1684.emploi: This verb appears 18 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and once in Acts. It is systematically used to recount the moments when Jesus or his disciples board a boat to cross a sea or a lake. The word particularly recurs in the accounts of crossing the Sea of Galilee: Jesus "went into the boat" before calming the storm (Matthew 8:23), and the disciples embarked without him while a crowd remained on the shore (John 6:22). The verb is always followed either by "into the boat" (εἰς πλοῖον) or simply by the complement indicating the embarkation. It is a verb of action, of movement: it describes a precise moment in the narrative, the moment of leaving solid ground.
G1684.portee: For the reader, this verb highlights a detail often overlooked: the life of Jesus and his disciples includes ordinary travels, journeys by sea, moments of real fatigue and risk — like during the storm. These small words remind us that Jesus engaged in concrete humanity, making his journeys like everyone else. This makes the picture of the Gospels more vivid and touching: we see Jesus moving, traveling, boarding as we would.

sens: To launch or propel something towards a place or inside something
To project someone into a place of punishment or torment
G1685.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to throw means to launch or propel something. The word is composed of the preposition "en" (ἐμ-) and the verb "to throw" (βάλλω), which reinforces the idea of projecting towards the inside or a specific place.
2. In a spiritual and judicial context, "to throw" takes on a fearsome meaning: it is to project someone into a place of punishment. In Luke 12:5, Jesus speaks of the one "who has the power to throw into hell" — this verb evokes the violence of divine judgment, God's absolute power over the fate of the wicked. It is an act of definitive and terrible condemnation.
G1685.origine: The word is formed from the preposition ἐμ ("in") and the verb βάλλω ("to throw, to cast"). This composition reinforces the idea of projecting something or someone *towards* or *into* a place. In Hebrew, this type of action is often rendered by words like שׂוּם ("to put, to place"), which can also express the action of placing someone in a situation, notably a situation of judgment.
G1685.emploi: The verb ἐμβάλλω appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 12:5. Jesus uses it to describe the divine power of condemnation: that of God alone, who can "throw" souls into hell after death. This vocabulary of "throwing" fits within Jesus' teaching on the fear of God — not the fear of man or of persecutors, but the sacred respect before God's eternal judgment. The context shows that this is not an arbitrary action, but the exercise of divine judicial power.
G1685.portee: This verb reminds the believer that God's judgment is real and fearsome. It is not about minimizing eternal punishment, but placing it at the heart of the fear of God — a fear based on respect for God's holy and just character, not on fear of men. It is a call to seriousness in the face of spiritual and eschatological realities.

sens: To immerse a part of the body or an object in a liquid
To briefly immerse the hand in a dish of food
To associate with someone in a common action or betrayal
G1686.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of plunging something into a liquid, so as to immerse or cover it. It is a precise and generally brief movement. In Matthew 26:23, Jesus speaks of the one who dips his hand in the dish with him: this image evokes the intimacy of a shared meal, the simple gesture of a guest who dips his bread or hand into the same common dish.
2. The expression "to put the hand in the dish" (literally "to dip the hand in the dish") refers to an act of intimacy at the table, but also, in context, to complicity or participation in an action: the one who shares this gesture will share a fate — here, betrayal. As Jesus says, it is the one who dips his hand with him who will betray him (Matthew 26:23 and Mark 14:20).
G1686.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "em" ("in") and "baptô" ("to dip" or "to plunge"). We find "baptô" in the verb "baptizô" (to baptize), which originally means "to immerse." The family of the word refers to the fundamental image of immersion or the impregnation of one substance in another.
G1686.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two parallels of the last supper of Jesus with his disciples. In these two passages (Matthew 26:23 and Mark 14:20), Jesus uses this image to designate the one who will betray him. The gesture of dipping his hand in the dish with Jesus is that of a companion, a friend, which makes the betrayal all the more serious: it comes from someone who shared his bread, who was seated at his table.
G1686.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the hidden meaning of gestures. A simple act of the meal becomes the image of a radical breach of trust: the one who dips his hand in the dish with Jesus is destined by friendship, but will betray him. It reminds us that even in intimacy, even in the most ordinary gestures of sharing, betrayal can sprout.

sens: To take possession of something by grabbing it
To usurp a position, a right, a reward that belongs to someone else
To dominate someone by exercising abusive or fraudulent authority
G1687.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of seizing or taking something that does not belong to you — a theft or spoliation. In Colossians 2:18, the apostle Paul warns the Christians in Colossae: some false teachers seek to "seize" the prize of the race, that is, to deprive them of the reward promised on the day of judgment. These seducers behave like robbers who take away your possessions.

2. More broadly, the word designates the action of usurping what legally belongs to another — a function, a title, a dignity. It is to fraudulently seize what does not rightfully belong to you.

3. Finally, the word can express abusive domination, a coercive grip: the one who "seizes" imposes his authority unjustly and tyrannically, disregarding the free consent of his victim.
G1687.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that means "to walk on" or "to enter into" (ἐμ- = in, into; βαίνω = to walk). The meaning has shifted from physical movement to appropriation, then to usurpation. The word first evokes one who enters without right into a property or charge, then one who seizes it and retains it against the legitimate owner. This evolution from the concrete to the figurative is very common in Greek vocabulary.
G1687.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Colossians 2:18. Paul uses it to describe the tactics of the false teachers who were active in the church of Colossae. These men, under the pretext of humility and worship of angels, sought to divert young Christians from their walk toward Christ and to "seize" their eternal crown. The context is one of religious seduction: it is not a physical violence, but a spiritual manipulation that usurps apostolic authority and the assurance that the believer has in his redemption.
G1687.portee: This word warns the Christian reader that there are powers and teachers who seek to divert him from his race toward Christ and to take away his crown, that is, his heavenly reward and assurance in God. It invites vigilance against religious seductions—those that promise superior wisdom or deeper spirituality, but which divert us from the simple Gospel. Remaining attached to Christ is to preserve the prize of the race.

sens: To place someone or something on a ship, to install on board
To embark (one or more people on a boat)
G1688.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to put in" or "to bring in," but in a maritime context, it takes on the precise meaning of installing or loading on board a ship. In Acts 27:6, the centurion "made us board" the ship of Alexandria: it refers to the concrete and physical action of embarking prisoners and their guards.
2. It is the boarding itself, the act of bringing people or materials on board a boat for the crossing. The verb emphasizes the administrative or military action of the responsible person who orders or executes this boarding.
G1688.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "em-" (in, into) and "bibazō" (to put, to place), which comes from a root meaning "to walk" or "to go." This composition paints the image of "bringing in," especially into a ship. The Hebrew word רָכַב ("to mount," "to ride") translated by this verb in ancient Greek in Hebrew texts shows how boarding is seen as a rising, an elevation.
G1688.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:6, during Paul's journey to Rome. In this passage, Paul and other prisoners are "boarded" onto an Egyptian ship heading to Italy, under the guard of the centurion Julius. This historical and concrete context — a real maritime journey with people and ships — remains the only use of the term in Scripture.
G1688.portee: This simple verb reminds us that in the narrative of Acts, even the practical details of Paul's journey — how to board, how to embark — are worthy of mention. It underscores the historical reality of the journey and imprisonment of Paul, and shows how God guides his servant through concrete circumstances, including the ordinary gestures of life at sea.

sens: to fix one's gaze on someone or something
to observe attentively, to examine
to contemplate with attention or emotion
to consider, to reflect on
G1689.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to direct one's gaze towards a person or object, often by fixing it intensely. In Mark 8:25, the healed blind man "looked intently" and "saw everything clearly": the word expresses that moment when vision becomes clear and precise. In John 1:36, the disciple "was looking at Jesus as He walked by" — a gaze that recognizes and focuses on someone.

2. In several passages, to look also means to examine or observe with a certain intention. Luke 20:17 states that Jesus "looked at" His adversaries before asking them a difficult question: this is not a mere glance, but the observation of a situation.

3. To look can also express a feeling or emotion that accompanies the gaze. In Mark 10:27, Jesus "looked" at His disciples before saying, "With men it is impossible, but not with God": this gaze conveys compassion or determination.

4. Figuratively, to look means to consider, to reflect on something. Matthew 6:26 tells us: "Look at the birds of the air" — it is an invitation to observe them to draw a lesson about divine providence.
G1689.origine: The word comes from the preposition ἐμ ("in") combined with the root βλέπ- ("to see, to look"). This root appears in other Greek words such as ἀβλεψία (blindness) or προβλέπω (to foresee). In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), ἐμβλέπω often translates Hebrew verbs like רָאָה (to see, to look) or פָּנָה (to turn one's face towards). The basic image is that of a movement of the gaze, focused and deliberate, rather than a mere glance.
G1689.emploi: The verb appears about 12 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels. Mark and Luke readily use it to describe Jesus' gazes: He "looks" at His disciples (Mark 10:27), He "casts His gaze" on those who press Him with questions (Luke 20:17), He "looks" at Peter after the denial (Luke 22:61). John uses it for the moment when John the Baptist "was looking at Jesus as He walked by" (John 1:36). Matthew uses it figuratively: "Look at the birds of the air" (Matthew 6:26) invites contemplation of creation to understand God's goodness. In Acts 1:11, the apostles are invited not to remain "looking up into heaven," meaning not to lose themselves in passive contemplation. The word always emphasizes a fixed gaze, never a mere glimpse.
G1689.portee: This verb reminds us that the gaze, in the Gospel, carries spiritual meaning. Jesus' gazes — of compassion, challenge, knowledge — are not indifferent; they touch and transform the one who is the object of them. When we are invited to "look," it is to learn to see as God sees: with attention, with intention, and often with a lesson of trust in providence. It is also a call not to remain passive, but to truly observe the world that God has created.

sens: to express deep indignation or anger
to address someone with a firm reprimand or urgent prohibition
to feel intense inner agitation in response to the suffering of others
G1690.detail: 1. The word first evokes the snorting or blowing of an angry horse — an image of brute force expressed violently. In Mark 14:5, the disciples become indignant against the woman who poured precious perfume on Jesus: it is a reaction of indignation, a rising anger. 2. Jesus uses this word when He admonishes the blind (Matthew 9:30) or the leper (Mark 1:43) by sternly forbidding them to speak of their healing. It is not a mere recommendation, but a firm order, a reprimand that carries the full authority of the Master. 3. In John 11:33 and 11:38, when Jesus visits Lazarus' tomb, Scripture says He was deeply moved within Himself. This is not anger, but a profound emotion in response to death and human suffering — an agitation of the soul in the face of the reality of mourning.
G1690.origine: The word comes from a root (βρίμη) that means force or violence. The base verb, βριμάομαι, describes the snorting or neighing of an irritated horse. The prefix ἐν (en) intensifies the action. The starting image is therefore one of a force expressed brutally — hence the general idea of manifesting a strong emotion, whether it be anger or compassion, always with depth and intensity.
G1690.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, mostly in Mark. In three passages (Matthew 9:30, Mark 1:43, Mark 14:5), it expresses indignation, anger, or severe prohibition. Jesus uses it to firmly command the healed to silence. The disciples use it when they reproach the woman for her act. In the other two passages (John 11:33 and 11:38), the meaning deepens: the verb describes Jesus' intense emotion in response to Lazarus' death, a spirit agitation that is less angry than compassionate. The context thus determines the nuance: anger, severe reprimand, or deep emotion.
G1690.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that Jesus is not indifferent. He is moved with indignation in the face of evil or lack of faith (Mark 14:5), He acts with firm authority when He commands silence (Mark 1:43), and He deeply shares in the pain of humanity before death (John 11:33). It is a lesson on the true humanity of Christ: not a divine apathy, but a soul that is moved, indignant, and compassionate with strength.

sens: to violently reject the contents of the stomach through the mouth
to reject something undesirable with disgust and repulsion
G1692.detail:
1. To vomit is to violently reject what one has in the stomach — an involuntary act of rejection by the body. This is the concrete image of the word.
2. In Revelation, Jesus uses this verb figuratively to express His absolute disgust: saying to the church of Laodicea, "I will vomit you out of My mouth" (Revelation 3:16) means that He cannot keep them, so repugnant is their lukewarm state. The image is deliberately crude to show the intensity of divine rejection.
G1692.origine: The verb ἐμέω comes from a Greek root that imitates the sound and gesture of vomiting. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses קֵא (qéa) with the same meaning, notably in Isaiah 19:14. It is an expressive word, painting the gesture rather than describing it abstractly.
G1692.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 3:16, where Jesus addresses a rebuke to the church of Laodicea. These lukewarm Christians — neither cold nor hot — inspire such disgust in Jesus that He compares them to something nauseating that He would spit out. It is a severe warning that uses the image of vomiting to express contempt and rejection.
G1692.portee: This word reminds us that spiritual lukewarmness provokes God's disgust. Jesus is not indifferent to a weak faith, without commitment — He actively rejects it. It is a call to sincerity and passion in our relationship with God: it is better to be "cold" (honest in one's unbelief) than lukewarm (pretending to have faith without truly adhering to it).

sens: To experience a violent and unrestrained fury towards someone
To act with a rage that drives one to persecute and mistreat
G1693.detail:
1. The verb describes an intense, almost bestial fury that seizes someone and dominates them. It is the rage of a man who has lost all control over himself and acts as a brutal enemy. In Acts 26:11, Paul recounts how, before his conversion, he was seized by this fury against Christians.
2. This rage does not remain contained: it manifests itself through acts of malice and persecution. Paul's fury drives him to strike the disciples in the synagogues, to force them to blaspheme, to hunt them from city to city — it is a rage that unfolds in concrete and systematic violence.
G1693.origine: The verb is composed of the prefix ἐν (in) and μαίνομαι (to be mad, to be in a frenzy). The starting image is that of furious madness, an outburst that ravages the soul like a mental illness. This composition reinforces the idea of total fury, a rage that consumes from within.
G1693.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:11. Paul uses it to describe his own mental state before his encounter with Christ on the road to Damascus. He speaks of his "excessive fury" against the disciples — a word that encapsulates all the violence of his persecution: his obsessive determination to punish them in the synagogues, to force them to blaspheme, to pursue them to foreign cities. It is a word chosen to express not only anger but the madness that drove him.
G1693.portee: This word helps the reader understand the depth of Paul's transformation. He did not simply change his mind — he was stopped by Christ himself while he was consumed by a fury that controlled and lost him. His testimony shows us that even the worst hatred, even the rage that drives one to persecute, can be completely reversed by grace. It is an encouragement for all those who have been enslaved by anger.

sens: He whose name means 'God with us'
Name given to the child that the prophet Isaiah announces to Ahaz
Messianic title designating Jesus in the Christian tradition
G1694.detail:
1. Emmanuel (in Hebrew, 'God with us') is primarily a symbolic name, a promise that God inscribes in the existence of a child to come. It is the sign that God does not abandon his people but comes to dwell among them.
2. The prophet Isaiah announced it to King Ahaz as a sign of future deliverance: a child would be born, who would embody the saving presence of God. This promised name expresses a break, a new divine intervention in history.
3. Matthew 1:23 applies this title to the newborn Jesus, recognizing in him the fulfillment of this ancient promise: God comes to dwell among men in person, no longer just through the Law or the prophets. This is the heart of the Christian mystery of the incarnation.
G1694.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew עִמָּנוּאֵל (immanouel), composed of three elements: 'im' (with), 'anu' (us), 'el' (God). Literally: 'God with us'. It is a prophetic name forged by the very meaning it carries, rich in all the theology of divine presence. Isaiah 7:14 is its source in the Hebrew Old Testament.
G1694.emploi: Emmanuel appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:23. Matthew cites it word for word from the promise of Isaiah 7:14 (according to the Greek version of the Old Testament), and he comments: 'which means God with us'. This unique occurrence is decisive: it establishes the earliest Christian interpretation of the birth of Jesus. For Matthew, this child fulfills the promise that God would be present to his people, not in a dream or from afar, but in flesh and person.
G1694.portee: The name Emmanuel expresses the essence of the Christian faith: God is not distant, but he has come. This transforms the understanding of Jesus: he is not just another wise man or prophet, but God himself drawing near to humanity. For the believer, this means that in every trial and solitude, the promise remains: 'God with us'. It is a word of comfort and certainty.

sens: Village in Judea located about eleven kilometers from Jerusalem
G1695.detail:
1. Emmaus is a small village located about sixty stadia (one stadium measures approximately 185 meters, or about eleven kilometers) west of Jerusalem. It is there that the resurrected Jesus meets two disciples who are heading to this village and do not recognize him on the evening of his resurrection.
2. The exact site has been debated by ancient and modern geographers, but it corresponds to a small rural settlement well known at the time of Jesus, near Jerusalem.
G1695.origine: The Greek name Ἐμμαούς (Emmaous) transcribes a locality in Judea. The exact site has been debated by ancient and modern geographers, but it corresponds to a small rural settlement well known at the time of Jesus, near Jerusalem.
G1695.emploi: Emmaus appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:13, during the account of the appearances of the resurrected Jesus. It is in this village that one of the two disciples, Cleopas, recognizes Jesus at the moment of the meal, after the Lord has explained the Scriptures to them along the way. This account of the road to Emmaus is one of the most poignant in the Gospel.
G1695.portee: This account reminds us that the resurrected Jesus remains present with his disciples despite pain and doubt, and that he reveals himself to those who walk with him with a sincere heart and are attentive to his Word. The recognition of Jesus at the table, beyond physical appearance, underscores the depth of the relationship between the Resurrected and his disciples.

sens: to remain in a place, to stay physically
to hold firmly to a conviction, a commitment, an obligation without abandoning it
to faithfully observe a law, a commandment, an agreement
G1696.detail:
1. The simplest meaning is to be physically present somewhere, to stay there: Paul 'remained two whole years in a house he rented' in Rome (Acts 28:30). It is the same root as the verb 'to stay'.
2. But the word quickly enriches itself with a deeper meaning: to hold firm in a conviction or commitment, not to abandon it despite difficulties. Paul exhorts the disciples to 'persevere in the faith' (Acts 14:22), that is, to remain attached even 'through many tribulations'. It is to hold firmly to something without wavering.
3. In particular, the word means to remain faithful to an obligation, a law, an agreement. In the Greek Old Testament, it is found to speak of holding firm in covenant with God: 'they did not persevere in my covenant' (Hebrews 8:9). The one who 'observes' all the commandments of the law of Moses (Galatians 3:10) 'perseveres' in it — he remains faithful in practice.
G1696.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ἐν- ('in') and the verb μένω ('to stay, to remain'). It literally means 'to stay in'. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this verb often translates קוּם ('to rise', 'to stand'), which evokes the idea of holding firm, not falling, of persevering steadfastly. The family of μένω includes words like 'dwelling', 'inhabitant': all revolve around the idea of staying, of stability.
G1696.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament. It first describes a simple physical fact — Paul stays two years in Rome. But its three other uses concern spiritual perseverance: holding firm in faith in the face of tribulations (Acts 14:22), faithfully observing the commandments of the law (Galatians 3:10), or remaining faithful to a covenant with God (Hebrews 8:9). In this last context, the word emphasizes the reproach: Israel did not persevere in the covenant of Sinai. The word always joins the idea of staying with that of fidelity: one does not remain in something by chance, but by choice and attachment.
G1696.portee: This verb speaks to the heart of the disciple: faith is not a moment of emotion, it is a dwelling, a place where one chooses to stay. It requires 'perseverance', that is, to hold firm when circumstances become tough, like the disciples in the face of tribulations. It also means to concretely observe what one commits to — to keep the commandments, to remain in the new covenant — not as an external obligation, but as a fidelity at heart.

sens: Father of Shechem and chief of the Hivites
G1697.detail: Hamor is a Hivite chief mentioned in the Old Testament. His name appears in Acts 7:16 during Stephen's speech, where he recalls that Abraham purchased land at Shechem for the price of money paid "to the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem" — meaning that Abraham negotiated the purchase of the land with the family of this chief, whose son Shechem gave his name to the city.
G1697.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew חֲמוֹר (hamor), which literally means "donkey." It is a common Semitic name, borne by this Hivite chief whose story is found in Genesis 33 and 34. The Hivites were a Canaanite people established in the region of Shechem.
G1697.emploi: The name appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:16, in the speech that Saint Stephen delivers before the Sanhedrin. Stephen traces the history of the patriarchs and the covenant that God made with Abraham, recalling that the latter purchased land at Shechem to bury his family — a purchase made from the descendants of Hamor. This reference points back to the accounts in Genesis (chapters 33 and 34) where Hamor and his son Shechem play a central role in the relations between Jacob and the Canaanite peoples.
